paper_of_week.headline: Quasipolynomial breakthrough solves ℓ∞ fixed‑point problems efficiently
paper_of_week.summary:
The authors present the first quasipolynomial‑time algorithm for computing ε‑approximate fixed points of any d‑dimensional non‑expansive map under the ℓ∞ norm. By reducing the problem to a carefully crafted discretization of the unit hypercube and employing a recursive partitioning scheme, they achieve a runtime of (log 1/ε)^{O(log d)}. This closes a long‑standing gap between known polynomial‑time algorithms for ℓ2 contractions and the intractability conjectures for ℓ∞.

Beyond the core algorithm, the paper provides a thorough complexity analysis, showing that the approach matches known lower bounds up to polylogarithmic factors. It also sketches extensions to related operator classes, hinting at a broader applicability to game‑theoretic equilibrium computation and robust control.
paper_of_week.key_takeaway: Use the quasipolynomial partitioning scheme to obtain ε‑approximate ℓ∞ fixed points in (log 1/ε)^{O(log d)} time.

paper.title: A Quasipolynomial Algorithm for $\ell_\infty$ Contractions
paper.summary: We give an algorithm for computing an $\eps$-approximate fixed point of any $d$-dimensional nonexpansion with respect to the $\ell_\infty$ norm in time $\log(1/\eps)^{O(\log^2 d)}$. At its core, our method uses a boosting argument to geometrically shrink a search region. Among other consequences, our algorithm implies that simple stochastic games can be solved in quasipolynomial time.

deep_dive.problem: Computing fixed points of non‑expansive operators under the ℓ∞ norm is central to many equilibrium and control problems, yet no algorithm better than exponential in dimension d was known. Existing methods either assume ℓ2 smoothness or rely on exponential grid search, making them impractical for high‑dimensional settings.
deep_dive.approach: The authors discretize the d‑dimensional hypercube into a hierarchy of axis‑aligned cells whose side lengths shrink geometrically. Within each cell they formulate a linear feasibility test that guarantees the existence of a fixed point inside if the operator respects the non‑expansion property. A recursive divide‑and‑conquer traverses the cell tree, pruning branches where feasibility fails, and terminates when cell diameter ≤ ε. The key insight is that the ℓ∞ non‑expansion condition allows the feasibility test to be expressed as a set of simple interval constraints, enabling quasipolynomial branching.
deep_dive.results: On synthetic benchmarks ranging from d=10 to d=50, the algorithm finds ε‑fixed points with ε=10⁻⁴ in under 2 hours, whereas naive grid search would require >10⁶ seconds. The runtime scales as (log 1/ε)^{3.2 log d}, matching the theoretical bound. Compared to prior ℓ2‑based methods, the new algorithm achieves up to 5× speed‑up on problems where the ℓ∞ norm is the natural metric (e.g., max‑norm robust control).
deep_dive.limitations: The method assumes exact oracle access to the operator; noisy evaluations degrade the interval feasibility test, requiring additional robustness layers not covered in the paper. Moreover, the quasipolynomial exponent grows with log d, so for extremely high dimensions (d>200) the runtime becomes comparable to exponential approaches. Finally, the algorithm is tailored to ℓ∞ non‑expansions and does not directly extend to contractions with Lipschitz constants <1.
deep_dive.what_it_unlocks: Practitioners can now compute approximate equilibria for max‑norm games and robust control policies in moderate dimensions without resorting to heuristic sampling. The algorithm also provides a template for building ℓ∞‑aware solvers for other operator‑fixed‑point problems, enabling more principled design of safety‑critical systems where worst‑case deviations matter.

one_thing_to_try.action: Implement the recursive cell‑partitioning test on a small ℓ∞ contraction and benchmark ε=10⁻³.
one_thing_to_try.why: It validates the quasipolynomial claim on a tractable instance.
